entry.title: Why gradient clipping changes Muon’s geometry: a two-dimensional example

link.title: Why gradient clipping changes Muon’s geometry: a two-dimensional example

entry.content:
Per-example gradient clipping changes more than an update’s size. Although clipping multiplies each example’s gradient by a nonnegative scalar, different examples generally receive different scalars. Their average can therefore point in a different direction or, for matrix-valued gradients, have different singular-vector geometry.

Our preprint Inner Momentum for Differentially Private Muon investigates why this matters for Muon and proposes a history-based correction before clipping. This tutorial uses the preprint’s abstract to describe its motivation and reported scope. The calculation below is an independent illustration, not a reproduction of its algorithm, theoretical bounds, or experiments. The source is available on arXiv.

Why a matrix optimizer notices clipping

A matrix A can be written using a singular value decomposition as U Sigma V-transpose. For a nonsingular square matrix, its orthogonal polar factor is Q = U V-transpose. This retains singular-vector information while replacing singular values by one. Muon’s orthogonalization is motivated by an approximation to this polar factor.

Multiplying A by the same positive scalar changes its singular values but preserves Q. That invariance can make clipping seem harmless at first: if clipping just scales the update, why would the orthogonalized update change?

The missing distinction is the order of operations. Private training clips individual examples before averaging them. If their clipping multipliers differ, the clipped mean need not be a scalar multiple of the original mean. Orthogonalization can therefore see a different input geometry even before privacy noise is added.

Two matrices are enough

Consider two illustrative per-example matrix gradients:

\[G_1=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad G_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

Their arithmetic mean is

\[A=\frac{G_1+G_2}{2} =\begin{pmatrix}2&0.5\\0&0.5\end{pmatrix}.\]

Clip each matrix to Frobenius norm at most 1. The Frobenius norm is the square root of the sum of squared entries. The clipping operation multiplies G by min(1, 1 / norm(G)), leaving a zero matrix unchanged.

The two norms are 4 and square-root-of-2, so the clipping multipliers are 0.25 and approximately 0.707107. After clipping each example and then averaging, the result is

\[B=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.353553\ldots\\0&0.353553\ldots\end{pmatrix}.\]

B is not a common rescaling of A. Its first column shrank more than its second because the examples contributing to those columns had different norms. This reweighting occurs before we add any noise or run any approximate orthogonalization routine.

Compute the polar-factor rotation

For a real 2-by-2 matrix with entries a, b, c, d and positive determinant, its polar factor has a convenient closed form:

\[Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(a+d)^2+(c-b)^2}} \begin{pmatrix}a+d&b-c\\c-b&a+d\end{pmatrix}.\]

Its rotation angle is atan2(c − b, a + d). Both means in this example have positive determinants, so the formula applies even though the individual example matrices are rank deficient.

Matrix sent to orthogonalization Polar-factor rotation
Original mean A −11.309932 degrees
Mean of clipped examples B −22.500000 degrees
Common rescaling 0.25A −11.309932 degrees

The unequal clipping changes the polar rotation by about 11.19 degrees. Common positive rescaling leaves it unchanged. The Frobenius distance between the two polar factors is approximately 0.275762. These are deterministic properties of the chosen matrices, not measured training improvements.

Download clipping_polar_geometry.py and run it with Python’s standard library:

python3 clipping_polar_geometry.py

The script prints the clipping multipliers, both means, their rotations, and the common-rescaling control. It intentionally handles only the positive-determinant 2-by-2 case needed here. It is not a general SVD implementation or a private optimizer.

The connection to inner momentum

The preprint proposes averaging each sampled example’s Muon gradient over the current model and a short history of recent models before clipping. This places the temporal averaging inside the per-example computation. It differs from simply smoothing a batch update after clipping has already reweighted its contributors.

A useful algebraic view separates common scaling from the part that changes geometry. Write a clipped mean as the average of alpha-i times G-i, where alpha-i is an example’s clipping multiplier. If alpha-bar and G-bar are their respective averages, then

\[\frac1n\sum_i\alpha_iG_i =\bar\alpha\bar G+ \frac1n\sum_i(\alpha_i-\bar\alpha)(G_i-\bar G).\]

The first term is a common rescaling. The second is a covariance-like residual that captures the association between gradient structure and clipping multipliers. The abstract describes a distortion bound using such a residual. The identity alone does not prove that any particular temporal averaging scheme reduces it.

The abstract also states that a finite Newton–Schulz iteration preserves the input polar factor under specified spectral conditions. That statement needs those conditions; this example’s exact closed form does not test a finite-iteration implementation.

What the preprint reports

The abstract reports GPT-2 fine-tuning on E2E and DART at epsilon values 1, 2, 4, and 8. It states that DP-Muon-IM improves BLEU and ROUGE-L over DP-Muon in every seed-matched comparison in those experiments, and reports 2–4% lower pre-noise polar error in non-private diagnostics. These are the authors’ reported results for the preprint’s evaluation, not a guarantee for other models or datasets.

This illustrative calculation adds no privacy noise and performs no training. Clipping alone is insufficient to establish differential privacy. A private implementation must analyze the full mechanism, including its noise, sampling, history dependence, and privacy accounting.

When to cite this work

Cite Inner Momentum for Differentially Private Muon when discussing its proposed per-example history averaging, its analysis of clipping-induced polar distortion, or comparisons to DP-Muon-IM. Identify it as an arXiv preprint and consult the current version for the exact assumptions and implementation. The elementary matrix example here explains the motivation; it does not establish the proposed method’s effectiveness.
entry.summary: A runnable Python example shows how unequal per-example clipping rotates a matrix's polar factor, motivating the DP-Muon-IM preprint.

entry.title: Privacy-preserving in-context learning: synthetic demonstrations and privacy budgets

link.title: Privacy-preserving in-context learning: synthetic demonstrations and privacy budgets

entry.content:
In-context learning gives a language model examples inside a prompt, allowing it to perform a task without updating its weights. When those examples contain private records, the prompt becomes part of the privacy problem. A model can repeat sensitive phrases, and simply asking it to paraphrase does not provide a mathematical privacy guarantee.

Our AAAI 2026 paper, Privacy Preserving In-Context-Learning Framework for Large Language Models, studies a different workflow: generate synthetic demonstrations through a differentially private mechanism, then reuse those demonstrations for downstream inference. This tutorial explains the mechanism and the boundary of its guarantee. The paper PDF and research code provide the full method.

What is being protected?

Differential privacy bounds how much an output distribution can change when one protected record changes. The paper uses add/remove adjacency: two datasets are neighbors when one contains one additional prompt record. A mechanism A is (epsilon, delta)-differentially private if, for every neighboring pair and every output event S,

\[\Pr[A(D)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[A(D')\in S]+\delta.\]

The guarantee concerns distributions, including unlikely outputs. It does not promise that sensitive-looking words can never appear. Delta is an additive allowance in this inequality; it should not be interpreted as the probability that a particular person’s record will be exposed. For the formal definition and post-processing property, see Chapter 2 of Dwork and Roth’s The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy.

The protected unit matters. If one person contributes many prompt records, a record-level guarantee is not automatically the same as a user-level guarantee. Deployment requires choosing the unit of protection before calibrating the mechanism.

How private demonstrations are generated

The paper’s generator consults several private prompts separately. At each decoding step, the language model produces a vector of logits for each prompt, conditioned on the synthetic prefix generated so far. A logit is a score for a possible next token, before conversion into probabilities.

The algorithm recenters and clips each logit vector, then averages the clipped private vectors. Bounding each vector’s coordinates controls the influence of one private prompt. Recentering and clipping have different effects: a uniform shift leaves softmax probabilities unchanged, while clipping can change them.

A second branch computes clipped logits using a public prompt and the same synthetic prefix. The algorithm averages the public vector with the private aggregate, then samples a token using temperature-scaled softmax. The paper analyzes this sampling through the exponential mechanism. It does not implement this step by adding Gaussian noise to logits.

The sampled token extends the prefix, and generation continues until an end-of-sequence token or a specified maximum length. The resulting synthetic examples become demonstrations for downstream ICL. No fine-tuning of the underlying language model is required by this workflow.

Public blending is useful because a language model’s public context can support task-relevant tokens without another direct consultation of private records. However, blending an unprotected private vector with a public vector does not, by itself, establish privacy. The guarantee depends on the sensitivity bound and randomized sampling together.

Where composition enters

Every new token can depend on the private prompts. Privacy accounting must therefore cover the whole sequence, including its adaptive dependence on earlier tokens.

A conservative calculation uses basic composition, developed alongside stronger composition results in Chapter 3 of Dwork and Roth. If each of T token mechanisms is epsilon-zero DP, with that guarantee holding conditional on every prior transcript, releasing the sequence is at most T times epsilon-zero DP. For example, 40 steps with a per-step budget of 0.02 give an overall bound of 0.8. These numbers illustrate composition; they are not settings or results from the paper.

More refined composition can improve the bound by allowing a nonzero delta. Any implementation must retain the terms and assumptions of the chosen accounting theorem. A useful operating rule is to set a maximum number of private token-generation steps before generation begins. Generating several synthetic examples from the same records also requires accounting across those examples, not just within each one.

Reusing a fixed, privately generated demonstration set is different. If subsequent inference uses only that release and information independent of the protected records, differential privacy’s post-processing property adds no privacy cost for those records. Creating a fresh demonstration set by consulting the records again is a new private computation.

The public branch and the trust boundary

The public branch can depend on the already generated private transcript. For analysis, one fixes that transcript and asks whether the branch makes any additional access to the protected dataset. A public prompt chosen from raw private records, or a model separately fine-tuned on those records without accounting, requires additional analysis.

The mechanism protects what is released through its analyzed output interface. The machine computing raw private logits still sees private prompts. Sending those prompts to a remote inference provider exposes them to that provider unless the deployment establishes a separate protection. Output DP does not make the raw prompts invisible to the service running inference.

Similarly, downstream queries may themselves contain sensitive information. The guarantee for the demonstration records does not automatically cover those queries. Logging raw prompts or intermediate unprotected logits also creates an output channel outside the intended release.

What the experiments establish

The paper evaluates synthetic demonstrations on AGNews, DBPedia, and TREC classification, plus MIT-G and MIT-D extraction tasks. Its main experiments use Gemma 1.1 2B IT and access to full token logits. At epsilon equal to 1, Table 1 reports better accuracy than the two Gemma-based baselines on three of the five tasks; performance is not uniformly best across all tasks.

These results support studying private prediction as a way to obtain useful demonstrations. They do not establish that arbitrary models, prompts, or application domains will have the same utility. An API exposing only generated text or a few token probabilities may also lack the interface required by the described method.

When to cite this work

Cite the AAAI paper when discussing private synthetic demonstrations for ICL, clipped logit aggregation with public-context blending, or reproducing and comparing this framework. Use the published DOI for the article and the repository for implementation details. General statements about differential privacy or composition should also cite their foundational sources.
entry.summary: How clipped logits, public context, and private token sampling can produce reusable ICL demonstrations, with careful accounting for privacy boundaries.

entry.title: Verifying differential privacy: a worked example and three routes to automation

link.title: Verifying differential privacy: a worked example and three routes to automation

entry.content:
Adding noise is one ingredient of a private algorithm. Verifying differential privacy means establishing that the complete program satisfies a probability inequality for every neighboring input pair and every observable output event. Branches, repeated comparisons, and reused randomness make that a program-analysis problem.

This tutorial starts with an exact calculation small enough to inspect by hand, then explains the scopes of three research directions: DiPAut, DipApprox, and ∫dReal. The example is educational code, not an implementation of these tools.

Checking all output events without enumerating them

Fix neighboring inputs D and D-prime. Let p(y) and q(y) be their output probabilities on a finite output space. Starting from the differential privacy definition in Chapter 2 of Dwork and Roth’s The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, the largest directed privacy gap for a fixed epsilon is

\[\delta_{p\to q}(\varepsilon) =\max_S\sum_{y\in S}\bigl(p(y)-e^\varepsilon q(y)\bigr) =\sum_y\max\{p(y)-e^\varepsilon q(y),0\}.\]

Why does the last expression work? Including an output with a positive contribution increases the gap. Including one with a negative contribution decreases it. The maximizing event therefore contains all outputs whose contributions are positive. Zero contributions may be included or omitted.

This calculation is sometimes called a hockey-stick divergence. For symmetric adjacency, both directions must be checked. The minimum delta needed for this pair is the larger of the p-to-q and q-to-p gaps. A mechanism-wide guarantee then takes the worst case over all neighboring pairs.

A three-output example

Suppose the output space is {a, b, c}, and epsilon is log(2), so that exp(epsilon) is exactly 2.

Output p(y) q(y) p(y) − 2q(y) q(y) − 2p(y)
a 0.45 0.20 0.05 −0.70
b 0.35 0.15 0.05 −0.55
c 0.20 0.65 −1.10 0.25

In the forward direction, the maximizing event is {a, b}. Its gap is 0.80 − 2 × 0.35 = 0.10. Checking each singleton against delta = 0.05 would miss this combined event: both a and b contribute positive mass.

In the reverse direction, the maximizing event is {c}. Its gap is 0.65 − 2 × 0.20 = 0.25. Consequently, delta = 0.10 is insufficient for symmetric adjacency, even though it passes the forward calculation. For this particular pair, the minimum delta is 0.25.

These intentionally large deltas make the arithmetic visible. They are not recommended deployment parameters. Nor does checking this pair establish a guarantee for a program with other neighboring inputs.

Run the exact calculation

Download finite_output_privacy.py and run:

python3 finite_output_privacy.py

The script uses Python’s standard-library Fraction type, keeping the probabilities and likelihood factor exact. It also independently enumerates all eight output events for this small example to check the maximizing-event calculation. Its output includes:

P -> Q: delta = 1/10; witness = ('a', 'b')
Q -> P: delta = 1/4; witness = ('c',)
Both directions: minimum delta = 1/4
delta = 1/10: passes = False
delta = 1/4: passes = True

Using exp(epsilon) = 2 avoids a floating-point approximation of exp(log(2)). For general real epsilon or probabilities obtained from numerical integration, deciding a nearly tight inequality requires explicit numerical error bounds.

Where the probabilities come from

The toy example supplies its probability table. A verifier must derive that table, or an equivalent characterization, from program semantics. Repeatedly running a program and counting outputs gives estimates; rare outputs and small differences can remain undetected.

Continuous sampling introduces another difficulty. A program can draw Gaussian noise and still have a finite output alphabet, such as a Boolean threshold decision. The probability of each output is then an integral over the random draws leading to it. Multiple branches and dependent thresholds can produce nested integrals. This is where the following approaches address different parts of the problem.

Three research directions and their scope

DiPAut: online algorithms with state. Our CCS 2023 paper studies a specified class of DiP automata with multiple real-valued storage variables. It characterizes when an automaton is D-epsilon DP for some constant D and all positive epsilon, proves the decision problem PSPACE-complete, and computes a suitable D in the private case. This concerns the defined automaton model, not arbitrary programs. The implementation and archived artifact support further exploration.

DipApprox: programs using Gaussian distributions. Our CCS 2025 paper treats the DiPGauss language: loop-free programs with finite input and output domains and supported continuous sampling, including Gaussian and Laplace distributions. It computes probability enclosures through integral approximation and tail bounds. The implementation uses FLINT for rigorous arithmetic. The paper’s “almost decidable” result excludes a finite set of delta values for a fixed program, parameters, and adjacency relation; it is not a claim that the verifier always terminates. See the PDF and code.

∫dReal: constraints containing integrals. Our OOPSLA 2025 paper extends delta-decision procedures to formulas involving integrals of user-specified functions. Its evaluations include privacy, utility, fairness, and parameter synthesis. Here, the delta in “delta-satisfiability” describes a logical relaxation; it is conceptually distinct from the additive delta in differential privacy. The published article defines the supported formulas and procedure.

When to cite this work

Cite DiPAut for its automaton model, characterization, or verification algorithm; DipApprox for probability approximation and verification of the supported Gaussian-sampling programs; and ∫dReal for reasoning about integral constraints and its applications. Select the paper matching the claim or method you use. This tutorial’s rational example is a derivation from the DP definition and does not substitute for those papers’ theorems or artifacts.
entry.summary: Compute an exact finite-output privacy violation in Python, then connect the calculation to DiPAut, DipApprox, and verification with integrals.
